description.narrative: The overarching vision of the programme is a world with rich biodiversity and resilient ecosystems where people equitably enjoy their right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment, driven by a vibrant and pluralistic civil society for just and inclusive development. To contribute to this, the programme will focus on a set of global outcomes within five change areas: 1) CSO capacity and resilience; 2) civic space; 3) environmental and climate governance; 4) transforming economies; and 5) gender equality and social inclusion. The programme is built on a multi-sectoral approach to create systemic and transformative change, in which CSOs are the key agents of change. Building on learning and context: The programme builds on the strong results, track records and lessons learned from the previous Leading the Change (LtC) programmes and emphasises local ownership and impactful and trustful CSO partnerships. It will address three interdependent and non-linear problem areas, derived from the context and stakeholder analysis: Biodiversity loss and climate change; Weak democratic governance and shrinking civic space; Unsustainable economic development and inequitable market access. Aspects that will receive increased attention include the interlinkages between biodiversity loss and climate change, the interconnectedness between economic, social and democratic development related to natural resource governance, and civic space. The programme will contribute to the implementation of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and the Paris Agreement. Theory of change: The programme adopts a multi-dimensional and multisectoral approach to its Theory of change (ToC) with the key hypothesis that sustainable environmental and social transformation requires holistic, interconnected methods working with a variety of change areas and stakeholders. An equally important hypothesis is that CSOs with stronger capacities to act, influence and respond to the change areas will contribute to reducing environmental degradation, halting biodiversity loss and climate change. The CSOs are thus the primary actors for change and connectors to right holders in this programme. Key programme approaches and cross-cutting areas: The programme is grounded in an inclusive and human rights-based conservation approach that places people - especially Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and local communities - at the heart of conservation efforts. Partnerships, local ownership, learning and capacity strengthening, and innovation and system change are other key programme approaches. The latter includes innovation, and opportunities fund for creative problem-solving and exploring novel partnerships. The programme strives to promote gender equality through gender mainstreaming and targeted activities for womenâ€™s empowerment and transformation of gender norms. It will also integrate conflict sensitivity, and environment and climate perspectives. Partnerships and Local Ownership: The programme and its results will mainly be delivered through partnerships with a variety of different local CSOs, guided by local interests and priorities. These are formalised as either core, programme or project support. From the start, 25 % of all CSO partners are anticipated to be part of the core support modality, with the intent to increase this number during the programme period. Programmatic and project support will also be available to other CSOs, facilitating capacity streghthening and enhancing operational effectiveness. At least 60% of all programme funds will be transferred to the CSOs, with the aim of establishing agreements averaging 3.35 years, while one-year agreements with new partners remain a possibility. Values and principles for the equitable partnership model are established and worked upon. 3 Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL): The programme will use a MEL framework that improves results harvesting and strengthens the capacity for results-based management across all partners. Implementing a comprehensive and adaptive approach to MEL, combining indicator-based monitoring of progress with methods like outcome harvesting and collaborative learning events, will ensure that monitoring and evaluation is culturally sensitive, fosters mutual accountability, align with existing systems, and effectively capture and communicate the impact of the programme. Harmonisation and coordination: The WWF network actively fosters coordination among different donor-funded programmes to enhance synergies and minimise administrative burdens. Notably, synergies will be sought with existing WWF-led Sida programmes and the wider corporate sector. Programme management structure: At the global level, WWF Sweden will be responsible for the overall management of the programme, ensuring coordination and follow-up against the global results framework, and manages three sub-programmes. WWF partner offices will manage country level sub-programmes and be responsible for the partnerships with local CSOs. Operational management and internal control: The programme will benefit from a range of improvements made during the previous programme, including strengthened internal capacity, improved programme management processes, updated rules and routines, and revised organisational structures to better oversee internal governance and control, as well as facilitating formal decision-making. The WWF partner offices will have tools and processes in place to manage programme implementation and partnerships with CSOs. WWF Sweden uses established financial management systems and audit processes to uphold transparency and accountability. By implementing anti-corruption measures and proactive risk management, the aim is to build trust and integrity throughout the programme. Budget and Key ratios: Key ratio 1 is 62%, Key ratio 2 is 11% and Key ratio 3 is 16%. Of the total budget 86% covers costs for partners in ODA countries, while 14% covers costs in Sweden.
